title: Six phases, each building on the last
caption: Start from the prerequisites in other trees, then read the phases in order: a design method, reusable platform blocks, bounded problems, then complete stateful, regulated and organisation-scale systems. Each later phase assumes the contracts and failure vocabulary of the earlier ones.

title: Every edit lands in Room before the network sees it
caption: The UI writes the note and its outbox operation in one Room transaction and reads only Room. The sync engine drains the outbox to the Sync API and writes the server's answers back into Room. The server side is named, not designed.

title: The repository writes; workers sync; the UI reads Room
caption: The repository owns atomic local writes, while workers run durable push and pull without becoming alternate sources of UI state. The ViewModel's data arrives only through the notes Flow from Room.

title: Design the client; name the server boundary
caption: One diagram is enough: the Android client is the design scope, and it talks to a BFF or gateway that owns auth, routing and compatibility. Backend services appear only as named boundaries with black-box internals.

title: Start from the journey, end with a budget
caption: NFRs are not a recital. Start from the critical user journey, select only the dimensions that can change its design, and turn each one into a measurable budget, a failure policy and an accountable owner.

title: Performance is a coupled budget
caption: A user journey spends four budgets at once: rendering, memory, battery and network. An optimization is incomplete until its cost in the other three is measured on representative device tiers.

title: Services read meaning from semantics, not pixels
caption: Composables and Views expose roles, state, descriptions and actions to the framework accessibility node tree. TalkBack, Switch Access and other services read that tree and send the user’s focus and actions back through it, so the app must make the meaning explicit.

title: Stable string IDs connect copy to every locale
caption: Stable resource IDs carry product copy through the translation workflow into qualified resources. The build and App Bundle package them, Android picks the best match for the user’s locale at runtime, and the UI stays responsible for flexible, RTL-aware layout.

title: No device control proves trust alone
caption: The threat model and data classification decide five layers of device-side controls. Four of them produce signals the backend relies on, but the server still enforces credential lifetime, authorization, revocation and risk decisions.

groups.label: On the device and in the build

title: Three versions evolve on their own clocks
caption: The installed app, the wire contract and the local schema change independently, and installed clients cannot be assumed to upgrade. Compatibility controls combine all three to decide whether the user gets the full app, a degraded one, a migration, a warning or a block.

title: Only critical work runs before the first frame
caption: A cold start runs from the launcher tap through process creation, Application.onCreate and the first Activity to the first frame (TTID), then to content ready (TTFD). Non-critical initialization is queued during onCreate and runs after the first frame.

title: The browser signs in; the app only holds tokens
caption: The app sends an authorization request with a PKCE challenge through the system browser or a Custom Tab, where the user authenticates with the identity provider. The app exchanges the returned code and its verifier for tokens, stores them in the Keystore-wrapped vault and sends the access token to the API.

title: One refresher serves every 401
caption: The sign-in path runs from the UI through AuthRepository to Custom Tabs, the IdP API and the vault. On the request path, AuthInterceptor attaches the access token; a 401 goes to the single-flight TokenRefresher, which updates the vault and lets the interceptor retry once.

title: Verification decides who opens the link
caption: Android resolves the tapped HTTPS link. If the domain is not verified for this app, the browser or a user-selected handler opens it. If it is, the link router parses the URI into a typed route; a protected route with no session saves the route, authenticates, then navigates.

title: One router, one gate, one navigator
caption: LinkRouterActivity hands every ACTION_VIEW URI to DeepLinkParser, which returns a typed Route. AuthGate sends an authorized route straight to the Navigator; otherwise PendingRouteStore keeps it through the login flow and releases it to the Navigator after success.

title: Each push takes one of three paths
caption: The application server sends through FCM to the device, where FirebaseMessagingService applies the current app and message policy. A foreground app updates its own UI; durable work goes to WorkManager to refresh local data; a user-visible notification goes to NotificationManagerCompat, and a tap opens a validated deep-link route.

title: The dispatcher owns the delivery policy
caption: AppFcmMessagingService passes each FCM message to PushDispatcher, which chooses foreground presentation, a WorkManager refresh or an immediate notification built by NotificationFactory. Both the in-app path and the worker update the Room-backed inbox repository.

title: Reads come from memory; fetches never block them
caption: At startup the repository loads the last valid disk snapshot and publishes an immutable in-memory FlagSet, so typed evaluation is synchronous. A background fetch is validated and persisted atomically; the activation policy either swaps it in live or leaves it on disk for the next session.

title: A StateFlow of immutable snapshots
caption: Application.onCreate creates the FlagsRepository, which exposes the stored snapshot as a StateFlow that feature callers read. The background refresher fetches from the Flags API; the validator persists every valid response and swaps live-safe changes into the flow atomically.

title: Cached first, fetched second, activated by policy
caption: bootstrap() serves the last valid cached snapshot before any network call, so the app can evaluate synchronously. The background fetch is validated and persisted atomically; only a live-safe change is published to the running app, while a next-session change waits.

events.text: Live-safe: publish the new FlagSet. Next-session: keep the current snapshot.

title: Five signals, one policy, one flush path
caption: Crash, ANR, frame, network and startup capture all write to bounded event buffers. Priority, consent, sampling and redaction decide what is kept, and the FlushScheduler hands batches to a WorkManager FlushWorker that uploads to the ingestion API.

title: Crashes and perf data travel in separate lanes
caption: JVM, native and ANR failures go to CrashSink, which also snapshots the breadcrumb ring, and land in the critical durable store. Frame and HTTP metrics go to a sampled PerfSink and its own store. Both stores feed the same FlushScheduler and FlushWorker.

title: Queued events leave by ack, retry or deliberate drop
caption: Feature code calls typed Analytics.track, and consent, validation, redaction and sampling run before the event enters a durable, bounded queue. The scheduler triggers the FlushWorker. A success deletes the acknowledged batch, and a retryable failure backs off. Some events are dropped on purpose: a 400 or 422 batch or a single oversized event that can never succeed, and the oldest low-priority events when the queue overflows.

title: An interceptor chain guards the queue
caption: Every feature calls one Analytics API, and its interceptor chain applies the consent gate, schema validation, PII redaction and sampling before an event reaches the Room queue. The FlushScheduler and FlushWorker then send batches to the API.

title: Two caches, then the source
caption: A request tries memory, then disk, then the source. Bytes are decoded to the requested size only once they are found or fetched, then transformed, and the result fills the eligible cache tiers before it reaches the target.

title: One request through the pipeline
caption: A memory hit returns straight to the target. Otherwise the loader gets encoded bytes from disk or the network, decodes and transforms them, stores the eligible result in memory and returns it.

events.text: Memory hit: the memory cache returns the drawable to the target, and the request ends here.

title: Durable from enqueue to final file
caption: The queue and chunk progress live in Room, so a killed process can resume verified work. That needs Range support and a strong ETag; without them, the download restarts from zero. The final file appears only through an atomic assembly and rename, so a partial file is never presented as complete.

title: One worker, bounded chunks
caption: One worker owns the download’s state and fans out to a bounded set of chunks. Assembly begins only after every required chunk has passed validation.

title: One API, two bounded tiers
caption: The public cache coordinates two independently bounded tiers. Memory is there for latency. Disk keeps entries across restarts, and its data and index updates must stay recoverable after a crash.

title: Cheapest tier first; expired is a miss
caption: A read tries the cheapest tier first, and a fresh disk hit repopulates memory. An expired disk entry is a miss, not silently stale data.

title: An index beside opaque files
caption: The index owns lookup and eviction metadata. Opaque entry filenames keep raw keys out of the file system.

title: Room stays the UI’s source of truth
caption: The list reads through the Pager from Room. The mediator fetches from the cursor API and stores each page with its remote keys in one transaction, and the invalidated data drives rendering.

title: Load state belongs to the UI contract
caption: Items and load state travel together from the Pager through the ViewModel to the screen. Page rows and remote keys share a transaction, so a retry can’t corrupt the pagination boundary.

title: Three sources, one ranked list
caption: Only the latest query runs, so a stale response can’t replace newer text. Local and recent results keep latency low while the remote list is on its way.

title: Timing in the ViewModel, sources in the repository
caption: The ViewModel owns query timing and cancellation. The repository owns its sources, keeping request and cache policy out of composables.

title: The client owns the query, the server owns the ranking
caption: The client owns the query lifecycle, cached presentation and pagination. Ranking and facets stay a server contract rather than logic duplicated on the client.

title: Each query, a new generation
caption: Each accepted query creates a new paging generation, so old requests and results can’t leak into the current search.

title: Routing is a policy decision
caption: The router doesn’t map every event to every channel. It decides from the user’s preferences and consent, the locale, and the frequency and quiet-hours policy.

title: The inbox doesn’t depend on the push
caption: The local inbox renders offline. Read state is reconciled through the repository, so the screen isn’t coupled directly to push delivery or REST.

title: Policy before delivery, inbox either way
caption: Idempotency and policy run before any channel delivery. The inbox record doesn’t depend on whether a transient push, email or SMS attempt succeeds, and a channel that policy refuses still leaves a record.
